 LeBron Takes AI Betting App to Court Over Fake Endorsement
 “Defendants must face the legal consequences of their intentional conduct to prevent it from being repeated,” the lawsuit says. 
 By Ben Horney 
 Nov 17, 2026 | 06:20 pm 
 UPDATED Nov 18, 2026 | 08:38 am 
 Bill Streicher-Imagn Images

 Add Front Office Sports on Google 
 LeBron James has sued AI-powered sports betting app Bron AI over allegations the company turned his identity into a marketing tool for a product he never endorsed.
 The suit from James and LBJ Trademarks LLC, filed Tuesday in New York federal court , takes aim at PlayVision Inc., the parent company of Bron AI, as well as its two cofounders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby. It comes 12 days after James issued a cease-and-desist letter that railed against the “unauthorized use and illicit exploitation” of the 76ers star’s name, image, and likeness.
 James’s “endorsement is uniquely valuable,” the suit says. “And that is why Defendants decided to steal it.”
 Bron AI bills itself as a tool that aggregates data and odds from traditional sportsbooks and prediction markets, allowing users to identify potentially profitable wagers and automatically place bets on other apps. Its promotional video, which has since been removed from Bron AI’s social media accounts, featured a character resembling James and wearing a basketball jersey with his nickname, “Bron,” and his jersey number, 23. 
 James has “one of the most recognizable identities in the world,” the suit says, and he has “carefully protected his image.”
 Although Bron AI removed the video following the cease and desist, as of Tuesday evening the app’s name had not been changed; subsequent videos made light of the fact that its commercial caused controversy. Bron AI is currently teasing it will reveal a new name Wednesday .
 Representatives for Bron AI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
 The suit notes James is particularly sensitive to the fact that the ad gave the impression he was betting on NBA games, which is not allowed under NBA rules. It also highlights the fact that James has an exclusive partnership with Polymarket . It also says James owns common-law rights to the nickname “Bron,” which he has used since before he entered the NBA.
 The lawsuit is being brought not just to protect the rights of James, but also to highlight that AI tools now make it easy for companies to fabricate supposed endorsements of famous athletes “who never agreed to appear.” It notes other athletes were also featured in the Bron AI ad, including Luka Dončić, who similarly sent the company a cease-and-desist letter. 
 “The same tools can be turned on any athlete, at any level of the sport, with ease,” the suit says. “Defendants must face the legal consequences of their intentional conduct to prevent it from being repeated.”
 Although the ad was removed, James says the damage has been done because it was viewed more than 1 million times and is still available to watch via third parties. The suit also says the defendants have not complied with other demands from the cease and desist, including that they inform every person who has used the app, in writing, that James has no affiliation with the company. “Defendants’ conduct was willful, deliberate, and in bad faith,” the suit says.
 The complaint features seven counts, including false endorsement, trademark infringement, and deceptive acts and practices. It asks the court to order the defendants to disgorge any ill-gotten gains. It also seeks damages in an amount to be determined at trial, plus “corrective advertising expenses.”
 “Defendants’ conduct has deprived Mr. James of control over his own identity and reputation, falsely associated him with an unvetted betting product and with betting on NBA games, and confused the consuming public,” the suit says. “Those injuries cannot be fully measured or compensated by money damages.”
